extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, legal scholars, and educated public interested in political philosophy and limits of state power
extracted.subtask_description: Principled guidance on when society or the State may legitimately interfere with individual conduct (distinguishing self-regarding acts from acts affecting others), and related policy prescriptions (trade, policing, licensing, taxation, education).

rubrics_metrics.name: Free Trade doctrine / economic liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the cheapness and good quality of commodities are most effectually provided for by leaving producers and sellers perfectly free, under the solo check of equal freedom to the buyers for supplying themselves elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrictions on trade or production for trade are restraints and, qua restraint, an evil; they are wrong solely because they do not really produce the results desired. The principle of individual liberty is not directly involved in the doctrine of Free Trade; issues about limits of that doctrine (e.g., admissible public control to prevent fraud by adulteration) involve separate considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible public control for fraud, sanitation, worker protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Public control (e.g., prevention of fraud by adulteration, sanitary precautions, arrangements to protect workpeople in dangerous occupations) is in principle legitimate even though it affects part of conduct society can restrain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such questions involve liberty only insofar as leaving people to themselves is usually better, ceteris paribus, than controlling them; but legitimate control is undeniable where it prevents harm or fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition/Restriction that limits buyer access
rubrics_metrics.description: Interferences whose object is to make it impossible or difficult to obtain a particular commodity (e.g., Maine Law, prohibition of opium importation into China, restriction of sale of poisons) are essentially questions of liberty affecting the buyer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These interferences are objectionable not as infringements on producer/seller liberty but on the buyer's. Such prohibitions require special justification because they deny the buyer access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of police — preventive vs punitory intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an undisputed function of government to take precautions against crime before it has been committed as well as to detect and punish it afterwards; the preventive function is more liable to abuse than the punitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a public authority or private person sees someone evidently preparing to commit a crime, they may interfere to prevent it. Preventive interference should be carefully limited because many lawful freedoms could be represented as increasing facilities for delinquency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for intervention on imminent danger vs mere risk
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is certainty (or evident preparation) of imminent criminality, interference is permissible; when there is only danger of mischief, only the person can judge the sufficiency of motive and should generally be only warned, not forcibly prevented, unless the person is a child, delirious, or otherwise incapable of reflecting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: seizing and turning back a person attempting to cross a known-unsafe bridge is permitted when no time to warn; but in less certain cases, only warning should be given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionate regulatory measures to prevent misuse (informational vs burdensome)
rubrics_metrics.description: Precautions like labelling a dangerous drug may be enforced without violation of liberty; but requiring a medical practitioner's certificate in all cases would make access sometimes impossible or always expensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer informational and minimally intrusive measures (labels) over blanket, burdensome requirements (universal medical certificates) that block legitimate use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of formalities and recordkeeping as minimal safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalities (signatures, attestation of witnesses) and 'preappointed evidence' can be required to provide proof and deter fictitious contracts; similar minimal precautions may be enforced in sales of articles adapted as instruments of crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: seller required to register time, buyer's name/address, quality/quantity, ask the purpose and record the answer; require presence of a third person when no prescription. Such regulations should not materially impede legitimate access but should hinder improper use without detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance of self-regarding misconduct unless it threatens others
rubrics_metrics.description: Purely self-regarding misconduct ought not to be legally interdicted; the right to non-interference applies where the evil falls wholly on the agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ordinary drunkenness is not a fit subject for legislative interference; but if the agent, when drunk, has committed violence to others in the past, special legal restrictions or penalties when drunk are legitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsion to enforce legal duties to others
rubrics_metrics.description: Compulsory measures (including compulsory labour) are justified to force a person to fulfil legal duties to others (e.g., supporting his children) when no other means are available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Idleness alone is not punishable except in particular circumstances (public support, breach of contract); failure to perform duties to others may justify compulsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of public acts that violate decency
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts directly injurious only to the agent that are done publicly may be violations of good manners and thus fall within offences against others and may rightly be prohibited (e.g., offences against decency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicity converts some otherwise self-regarding acts into social offences; this provides principled ground for prohibiting public indecency without invading purely private conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to advise about self-regarding acts, limited when instigator has personal interest
rubrics_metrics.description: People ought to be free to give advice and inducements about acts that concern only the advised person; but where the instigator derives personal benefit (makes it his occupation to promote what society sees as evil), special considerations arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The State may legitimately attempt to exclude solicitations from interested instigators (pimps, gambling-house keepers) whose influence is not disinterested; restriction of public places or operators (not private mutual gambling) may be justified to exclude commercially interested promotion of harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fiscal measures to discourage harmful consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxation of stimulants and harmful commodities is admissible and may be approved up to the point producing the largest revenue, provided taxation choices consider which commodities consumers can best spare and which are injurious beyond moderation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxation for revenue is inevitable and unavoidably imposes penalties on consumption; the State should select, in preference, those commodities whose moderate use it deems positively injurious when used excessively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing and regulation of public places of resort
rubrics_metrics.description: Sale of potentially harmful commodities for consumption on the spot may be confined to persons of known or vouched-for respectability; hours and licence withdrawal can be regulated to enable public surveillance and to penalize keepers who permit breaches of the peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations concerning opening/closing hours, licence withdrawal for repeated breaches, and restriction to reputable keepers are fit to preserve public order in places prone to offences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection to limiting number of sale-places to restrict access
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting the number of beer and spirit houses for the express purpose of rendering them more difficult of access and diminishing temptation is, in principle, unjustifiable except where it treats labouring classes as children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such limitations assume paternalistic governance; a free society should avoid treating adult classes as wards and should rather focus on education and regulation as alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity and enforceability limits of voluntary engagements/contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: While persons may regulate by mutual agreement matters concerning only themselves, engagements that violate third-party rights or are injurious to the contracting party (e.g., selling oneself as a slave) are null and void and should not be enforced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The principle of liberty supports allowing voluntary acts, but it does not require enforcement of contracts that abdicate liberty or infringe others' rights; voluntary renunciation of liberty (to be free not to be free) is not to be enforced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal limits on personal-service contracts and moral obligations from reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts involving personal relations or services should not be legally binding beyond a limited duration; yet where one party has induced reliance, moral obligations arise that must be considered even if legal enforcement is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baron von Humboldt's view (no long binding personal-service contracts; easy dissolution of marriage) is noted but the text emphasizes that reliance and third-party consequences create moral duties that affect the fairness of unilateral retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: State duty to enforce a minimum standard of universal education
rubrics_metrics.description: The State should require and compel education up to a certain standard for every citizen; parents have a duty to provide such education, and the State should ensure fulfillment, at the parent's charge where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement could operate through public examinations (starting early and recurring annually), fines for noncompliant parents, state aid for those unable to pay, while avoiding State direction of educational content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid State monopoly of education; preserve diversity of education
rubrics_metrics.description: A general State education risks moulding people alike and establishing despotism over the mind; State education should exist, if at all, as one among many competing experiments, not as a sole controlling system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where private provision suffices, prefer voluntary education supported by compulsion to attend plus State aid over direct State control; State may step in only where society cannot otherwise provide proper institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of public examinations and limits on State influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Public examinations for compulsory education should test instrumental skills (e.g., reading) and confine higher required knowledge to facts and positive science; examinations on religion/politics should test that opinions are held and their grounds, not the truth of opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An annual examination regime with progressively broader subjects can enforce minimum knowledge and retention. Higher-branch examinations should be voluntary. The State should not use examinations to bias citizens' conclusions on disputed topics but may certify possession of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary higher examinations and neutral certificates
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher-branch examinations should be voluntary; degrees and public certificates should be given to all who pass but should confer no legal advantage beyond the weight of public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governments should not be allowed to exclude individuals from professions or careers on alleged deficiency of qualifications; certificates should indicate tested competence but not grant coercive professional monopolies.
